analysis.one_liner: Gives a federal regulator power to set safety standards for, inspect, and recall firearms and ammunition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in February 2001 with 27 Democratic cosponsors, it was sent to a House Judiciary subcommittee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have applied consumer-product-safety rules to guns and ammunition for the first time. A cabinet secretary could write design and performance safety standards, order recalls or refunds of defective or unreasonably dangerous guns, inspect factories and dealers, and fine or prosecute violations. It would also have required manufacturers to test and certify their products, put traceability labels on them, and required the government to collect and publish data on gun injuries and deaths.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to firearm injuries: buyers would get safety-tested, certified, labeled guns with the ability to compare products, owners of defective guns could get recalls or refunds, and anyone hurt by a rule-violating gun could sue for damages, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs.

how_it_helps.text: The Treasury Secretary must write regulations governing the design, manufacture, and performance of firearm products as reasonably necessary to reduce or prevent unreasonable risk of injury [S2] [S3].

The Secretary could order recalls, repairs, replacements, or refunds for products found defective, unreasonably risky, or out of compliance, and could bar manufacture, import, or sale of unreasonably risky products outright [S2] [S3].

Manufacturers would have to test and certify every firearm product, label it with maker, model, and date, and keep records open to inspection, so buyers and investigators could trace products [S2] [S3].

The government would collect, analyze, and publish data on the circumstances of firearm deaths and injuries and the economic costs, and report annually to Congress on enforcement and industry meetings [S2] [S3].

Anyone injured by a violation could sue for damages including consequential damages, and any interested person could sue to enforce the act, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs [S3].
The bill explicitly preserves stronger state gun laws and does not preempt them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would bear testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, inspection, and recall costs, plus fines up to $10,000 per product ($20,000 willful) after five years, and exposure to private lawsuits; some of these costs would likely be passed to buyers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives a single cabinet officer sweeping authority, including the power to prohibit manufacture or import of any product deemed unreasonably risky, which critics of gun regulation would see as a path to restricting firearms availability without a specific legislative vote [S3].

Its anti-stockpiling provision makes it unlawful to manufacture, purchase, or import a product at a rate significantly above a pre-regulation base period during the gap before a rule takes effect, a restriction on ordinary purchases with no counterpart in other consumer-safety law [S3].
Per-product civil penalties, mandatory testing and certification, and mandatory record-keeping would impose real compliance costs that manufacturers would likely pass on to buyers as higher prices.
Expanded private lawsuits, including suits by 'any interested person' even without personal injury, would increase litigation against manufacturers and dealers beyond injury cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is standard consumer-product-safety treatment for a product associated with tens of thousands of American deaths a year, and most of the machinery (testing, certification, recalls, labeling, injury data) mirrors what already applies to toys, cribs, and power tools. The weakest parts are the anti-stockpiling provision, which is an unusually blunt limit on lawful purchases during rulemaking windows, and the breadth of discretion given to one secretary over a constitutionally sensitive product. A narrower bill with the same recall-and-certify core would have carried the same public benefit at less cost and less litigation risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which passed it down to its Crime subcommittee three weeks later, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Kennedy of Rhode Island introduced the Firearms Safety and Consumer Protection Act of 2001 on February 14, 2001 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced [S5].
On March 2, 2001, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, which was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
Twenty-seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers came out ahead: they avoided federal safety standards, mandatory testing and certification, recall authority, factory and dealer inspections, per-product fines, and a new private right of action against them. Gun owners saw no change in the products available to them.

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a markup or a committee vote on the bill; it was passed down to the Crime subcommittee and never returned.

against.name: House Republican majority (223 of 223 House Republicans)
against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda and the Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the majority that controlled the committee and floor calendar allowed no action on it for two years.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 28 sponsors and cosponsors was a House Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee took no action beyond forwarding it to a subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's status as the only major consumer product category with no federal safety regulator, subjecting it to mandatory testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, inspections, recalls, per-product fines, and private lawsuits. Its interest in avoiding this regime ran directly against the public's interest in safer, traceable products and injury data.

The bill would have required dealers and pawnbrokers to maintain and open for inspection compliance records, imposed liability for selling unlabeled or noncompliant products, and exposed them to suits by 'any interested person.' The industry benefited from the bill's death by keeping the current light-touch federal regime in place.
